设计\\n\\n## 项目隔离\\n\\n本次创建唯一 run 根：\\n\\n`/Users/smkzw/Documents/AI Products/competitive-intelligence-acceptance/task-10.2-<run_id>/`\\n\\n其下为 `a-real`、`b-real`、`c-real` 三个开始时不存在的项目。测试先记录 run start、源码摘要、包摘要和空根证明，再调用唯一 CLI 创建项目。\\n\\n## 科学输入\\n\\n- A：特应性皮炎；完整创新药宇宙与全球/中国开发状态。\\n- B：阵发性睡眠性血红蛋白尿；疗效、安全性、基线、完成/退出/补救治疗/禁用药/方案偏离等披露状态。\\n- C：特应性皮炎；登记字段足够路径及关键临床设计字段缺失后的 Protocol/SAP 补件恢复路径。\\n\\n每条事实保留来源 URL、来源身份、首次披露/获取时间、定位、原值、规范化值和证据状态。结果数值不得因自动抽取空 `drug_name` 而丢失；必须从 trial/arm 身份回填映射后再核验。\\n\\n## 当前运行闭合\\n\\n每类 exact test 沿：\\n\\n`run_id → evidence/report snapshot → artifact manifest → artifact record → overview.html/详情页 → 双浏览器 verdict`\\n\\n检查 producer run、source/package digest、cutoff、coverage、文件 SHA-256/bytes/mtime、全部路由 anchor。旧 mtime、预存项目、旧 manifest、断链、伪浏览器 verdict 或只验证首页均失败关闭。\\n\\n## 故障处理\\n\\n零竞品、零方案、零结果、大面积数值缺失或页面空白均视为异常信号，先检查检索词、API/页面结构、登录/限流、解析器、身份映射、截止日和门槛，再判断是否确实未公开。两次相同失败无新证据时改变方法或来源，不机械重试。\\n--- implement ---\\n# Task 10.2 实施步骤\\n\\n- [ ] R01：冻结本次 All rights reserved, including those for text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies.</copyright-statement></permissions><self-uri xmlns:xlink=\\\"http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink\\\" content-type=\\\"pmc-pdf\\\" xlink:href=\\\"jamadermatol-e250982.pdf\\\"/><self-uri xmlns:xlink=\\\"http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink\\\" content-type=\\\"pdf-version\\\" xlink:href=\\\"jamadermatol-e250982.pdf\\\">jamadermatol-e250982.pdf</self-uri><self-uri xmlns:xlink=\\\"http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink\\\" content-type=\\\"silverchair\\\" xlink:href=\\\"https://jamanetwork.com/journals/archderm/fullarticle/10.1001/jamadermatol.2025.0982\\\"/><abstract abstract-type=\\\"key-points\\\"><title>Key Points</title><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-1\\\"><title>Question</title><p>What are the efficacy and adverse events of ivarmacitinib treatment in adolescents and adults with moderate to severe atopic dermatitis?</p></sec><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-2\\\"><title>Findings</title><p>This phase 3 randomized clinical trial of 336 patients (age ≥12 years) found that significantly more patients in the 4- or 8-mg ivarmacitinib groups achieved an Investigator Global Assessment score of 0 or 1 with at least a 2-grade improvement from baseline and an Eczema Area and Severity Index score improvement of at least 75% compared to the placebo group. Serious treatment-emergent adverse events occurred at low and similar rates across all groups.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-3\\\"><title>Meaning</title><p>These findings show that ivarmacitinib is an effective treatment with a favorable risk-benefit profile for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis in adults and adolescents.</p></sec></abstract><abstract><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-4\\\"><title>Importance</title><p>Ivarmacitinib, a selective oral Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) inhibitor, has demonstrated efficacy for treating adults with moderate to severe atopic dermatitis (AD) in a phase 2 trial.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-5\\\"><title>Objective</title><p>To evaluate the efficacy and adverse events of ivarmacitinib in adolescents and adults with moderate to severe AD.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-6\\\"><title>Design, Setting, and Participants</title><p>This multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 randomized clinical trial included patients aged 12 to 75 years with moderate to severe AD. Patients were enrolled from 53 sites in Canada and China from April 2021 to April 2022. Data were analyzed from July 11 to September 27, 2023.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-7\\\"><title>Interventions</title><p>Patients were randomized (1:1:1) to receive once-daily 4- or 8-mg ivarmacitinib or placebo for 16 weeks.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-8\\\"><title>Main Outcomes and Measures</title><p>Co-primary end points were the proportions of patients achieving an Investigator Global Assessment (IGA) score of 0 (clear) or 1 (almost clear) with at least a 2-grade improvement from baseline and an Eczema Area and Severity Index score improvement of 75% (EASI-75) at week 16.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-9\\\"><title>Results</title><p>Of 336 randomized patients (mean [SD] age, 31.1 [15.4] years; 213 [63.4%] male; 286 [85.1%] Asian), 113 received 4-mg ivarmacitinib, 112 received 8-mg ivarmacitinib, and 111 received placebo. At week 16, significantly more patients in the 4-mg ivarmacitinib group (41 of 113 [36.3%]; 95% CI, 27.5%-45.9%; <italic toggle=\\\"yes\\\">P</italic> &lt; .001) and the 8-mg ivarmacitinib group (47 of 112 [42.0%]; 95% CI, 32.7%-51.7%; <italic toggle=\\\"yes\\\">P</italic> &lt; .001) achieved an IGA score of 0 or 1 with at least a 2-grade improvement compared to the placebo group (10 of 111 [9.0%]; 95% CI, 4.4%-15.9%). EASI-75 responses were also significantly higher in the ivarmacitinib groups: 61 patients (54.0%; 95% CI, 44.4%-63.4%; <italic toggle=\\\"yes\\\">P</italic> &lt; .001) in the 4-mg group, and 74 (66.1%; 95% CI, 56.5%-74.8%; <italic toggle=\\\"yes\\\">P</italic> &lt; .001) in 8-mg group compared to 24 patients (21.6%; 95% CI, 14.4%-30.4%) in the placebo group. Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported by 78 patients (69.0%) in the 4-mg group, 74 (66.1%) in the 8-mg group, and 72 (64.9%) in the placebo group. Serious treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 3 patients (2.7%) in the 4-mg group, 2 (1.8%) in the 8-mg group, and 3 (2.7%) in the placebo group.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-10\\\"><title>Conclusions and Relevance</title><p>This phase 3 randomized clinical trial determined that once-daily ivarmacitinib demonstrated significant efficacy and a favorable risk-benefit profile for treating moderate to severe AD in adults and adolescents. These results support the potential of ivarmacitinib as a new therapeutic option.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-11\\\"><title>Trial Registration</title><p>ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: <ext-link xmlns:xlink=\\\"http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink\\\" xlink:href=\\\"https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04875169\\\" ext-link-type=\\\"uri\\\">NCT04875169</ext-link></p></sec></abstract><abstract abstract-type=\\\"teaser\\\" specific-use=\\\"electronic\\\"><p>This phase 3 randomized clinical trial evaluates the efficacy and adverse effects of ivarmacitinib for treatment of moderate to severe atopic dermatitis in adults and                    <div class=\\\"new-nr-zi\\\"><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">March 30, 2026 — Simcere Pharmaceutical Group Limited (2096.HK) announced that Phase III results from the RADIANT-AD study of rademikibart, an investigational monoclonal antibody developed in collaboration with Connect Biopharma, were presented as a Late-Breaking Abstract (LBA) oral presentation at the 84th Annual Meeting of the American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) in Denver, United States.</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">The study, led by co-principal investigators Professor Zhang Jianzhong and Professor Zhou Cheng of Peking University People’s Hospital, evaluated rademikibart in adults and adolescents with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis (AD). Results showed that rademikibart provided rapid relief of itch and improvement in skin inflammation within two weeks, along with high levels of skin clearance that were sustained through 52 weeks. The findings were presented by Professor Zhou Cheng on behalf of the research team on March 28.</span></p><p><br/></p><p style=\\\"text-align: center;\\\"><img src=\\\"https://www.simcere.com/attached/upload/image/20260330/6391046622404632308165209.jpg\\\" title=\\\"91da8495-d731-45a0-8498-71bd89595322.jpg\\\" alt=\\\"91da8495-d731-45a0-8498-71bd89595322.jpg\\\" width=\\\"500\\\" height=\\\"700\\\" border=\\\"0\\\" vspace=\\\"0\\\" style=\\\"text-align: center; text-wrap-mode: wrap; width: 500px; height: 700px;\\\"/></p><p style=\\\"text-align: center;\\\">Dr Zhou Cheng giving oral presnetation at the 84th AAD Annual Meeting</p><p><br/></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">Atopic dermatitis is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin disease characterized by recurrent eczematous lesions, severe dryness, and intense pruritus. It is estimated that approximately 70 million people in China are affected, with nearly half experiencing moderate-to-severe disease. Despite the availability of biologic therapies, disease management remains challenging, and there is a continued need for more effective and durable treatment options.</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">The randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase III trial (NCT06477835) enrolled 259 adult and adolescent patients with moderate-to-severe AD. Participants were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive rademikibart or placebo for 16 weeks, followed by a 36-week open-label extension during which all patients received rademikibart.</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">Efficacy Results</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">At Week 16, a significantly greater proportion of patients treated with rademikibart achieved key endpoints compared with placebo (p&lt;0.0001), including:</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">Investigator’s Global Assessment (IGA) score of 0 or 1 with a ≥2-point reduction from baseline (47.7% vs. 17.6%)</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">≥75% improvement in Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI-75) (74.2% vs. 34.4%)</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">≥90% improvement in Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI-90) (43.0% vs. 14.5%)</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">≥3-point reduction in Peak Pruritus Numerical Rating Scale (PP-NRS) (54.7% vs. 27.5%)</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">Efficacy was sustained and further improved through Week 52, with response rates reaching 87.1%, 96.6%, 85.3%, and 91.2% for the respective endpoints.</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">Safety</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">Rademikibart demonstrated a favorable safety profile over 52 weeks, consistent with other anti–IL-4Rα therapies.</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">At Week 16, the incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) was 60.9% in the rademikibart group and 64.9% in the placebo group. By Week 52, the overall incidence of TEAEs was 82.2%. Rates of serious adverse events (SAEs) and treatment discontinuations due to adverse events remained low throughout the study period.</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">Professor Zhang Jianzhong commented:</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">“Rademikibart demonstrates the dual advantages of strong efficacy and a favorable safety profile, with its long-term safety further strengthening clinical confidence. From a clinical perspective, its significance extends beyond providing a new treatment option; it has the potential to help raise treatment goals for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis and support standardized, long-term disease management.”</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">Professor Zhou Cheng added:</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">“Rademikibart showed the ability to deliver deep and sustained disease control in atopic dermatitis, with rapid onset and continuously improving efficacy over one year of treatment, without an apparent plateau. These findings address key challenges in long-term disease management and suggest that rademikibart may offer an effective and well-tolerated biologic option for patients.”</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">Rademikibart is a fully human monoclonal antibody targeting IL-4Rα. In preclinical studies, it has demonstrated high binding affinity and inhibits the signaling of both IL-4 and IL-13, key drivers of type 2 inflammation. By targeting this pathway, rademikibart is being developed for the treatment of inflammatory diseases including atopic dermatitis and asthma.</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">In November 2023, Simcere entered into an exclusive licensing and collaboration agreement with Connect Biopharma, obtaining rights to develop, manufacture, and commercialize rademikibart for all indications in China. The Phase III study was conducted across 59 clinical centers in China and successfully met its primary endpoint.</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">&nbsp;</span></p><p><span style=\\\"font-size: 20px;\\\">The Phase III results provide supportive evidence of rademikibart’s clinical profile. Serious treatment-emergent adverse events occurred at low and similar rates across all groups.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-3\\\"><title>Meaning</title><p>These findings show that ivarmacitinib is an effective treatment with a favorable risk-benefit profile for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis in adults and adolescents.</p></sec></abstract><abstract><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-4\\\"><title>Importance</title><p>Ivarmacitinib, a selective oral Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) inhibitor, has demonstrated efficacy for treating adults with moderate to severe atopic dermatitis (AD) in a phase 2 trial.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-5\\\"><title>Objective</title><p>To evaluate the efficacy and adverse events of ivarmacitinib in adolescents and adults with moderate to severe AD.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-6\\\"><title>Design, Setting, and Participants</title><p>This multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 randomized clinical trial included patients aged 12 to 75 years with moderate to severe AD. Patients were enrolled from 53 sites in Canada and China from April 2021 to April 2022. Data were analyzed from July 11 to September 27, 2023.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-7\\\"><title>Interventions</title><p>Patients were randomized (1:1:1) to receive once-daily 4- or 8-mg ivarmacitinib or placebo for 16 weeks.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-8\\\"><title>Main Outcomes and Measures</title><p>Co-primary end points were the proportions of patients achieving an Investigator Global Assessment (IGA) score of 0 (clear) or 1 (almost clear) with at least a 2-grade improvement from baseline and an Eczema Area and Severity Index score improvement of 75% (EASI-75) at week 16.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-9\\\"><title>Results</title><p>Of 336 randomized patients (mean [SD] age, 31.1 [15.4] years; 213 [63.4%] male; 286 [85.1%] Asian), 113 received 4-mg ivarmacitinib, 112 received 8-mg ivarmacitinib, and 111 received placebo. At week 16, significantly more patients in the 4-mg ivarmacitinib group (41 of 113 [36.3%]; 95% CI, 27.5%-45.9%; <italic toggle=\\\"yes\\\">P</italic> &lt; .001) and the 8-mg ivarmacitinib group (47 of 112 [42.0%]; 95% CI, 32.7%-51.7%; <italic toggle=\\\"yes\\\">P</italic> &lt; .001) achieved an IGA score of 0 or 1 with at least a 2-grade improvement compared to the placebo group (10 of 111 [9.0%]; 95% CI, 4.4%-15.9%). EASI-75 responses were also significantly higher in the ivarmacitinib groups: 61 patients (54.0%; 95% CI, 44.4%-63.4%; <italic toggle=\\\"yes\\\">P</italic> &lt; .001) in the 4-mg group, and 74 (66.1%; 95% CI, 56.5%-74.8%; <italic toggle=\\\"yes\\\">P</italic> &lt; .001) in 8-mg group compared to 24 patients (21.6%; 95% CI, 14.4%-30.4%) in the placebo group. Treatment-emergent adverse events were reported by 78 patients (69.0%) in the 4-mg group, 74 (66.1%) in the 8-mg group, and 72 (64.9%) in the placebo group. Serious treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 3 patients (2.7%) in the 4-mg group, 2 (1.8%) in the 8-mg group, and 3 (2.7%) in the placebo group.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-10\\\"><title>Conclusions and Relevance</title><p>This phase 3 randomized clinical trial determined that once-daily ivarmacitinib demonstrated significant efficacy and a favorable risk-benefit profile for treating moderate to severe AD in adults and adolescents. These results support the potential of ivarmacitinib as a new therapeutic option.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"ab-doi250014-11\\\"><title>Trial Registration</title><p>ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: <ext-link    return unescape(encodeURIComponent(str)).length;\\nfixtures/positive/a-atopic-dermatitis/sources/ssgj611-nct05544591-pmc.xml:3:</p></sec><sec id=\\\"Sec1\\\"><title>Introduction</title><p id=\\\"Par7\\\">Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by eczematous lesions and intense pruritus. In Chinese adults, the 1-year prevalence of adult AD was 6.13%, and the point prevalence of AD was 2.42% [<xref ref-type=\\\"bibr\\\" rid=\\\"CR1\\\">1</xref>]. The point prevalence of AD based on clinical diagnosis by dermatologists was 12.94% overall, ranging from 9.00% to 24.69% between metropolises for preschool children in China [<xref ref-type=\\\"bibr\\\" rid=\\\"CR2\\\">2</xref>–<xref ref-type=\\\"bibr\\\" rid=\\\"CR4\\\">4</xref>]. The pathogenesis of AD involves a complex interplay between environmental and genetic factors, resulting in immune dysregulation [<xref ref-type=\\\"bibr\\\" rid=\\\"CR5\\\">5</xref>]. Major immune abnormalities include allergen presentation, T-helper 2 cell (Th2)-driven responses, impaired regulatory T cells, excessive immunoglobulin E (IgE) production, and increased eosinophils [<xref ref-type=\\\"bibr\\\" rid=\\\"CR6\\\">6</xref>–<xref ref-type=\\\"bibr\\\" rid=\\\"CR10\\\">10</xref>]. Type 2 inflammation, primarily mediated by interleukin (IL)−4 and IL-13, is thought to play a central role in AD pathogenesis [<xref ref-type=\\\"bibr\\\" rid=\\\"CR11\\\">11</xref>]. Elevated IL-4 and IL-13 levels are associated with AD severity, facilitating IgE production, macrophage activation, eosinophil recruitment, and pruritus through IL-4Rα signaling in neurons [<xref ref-type=\\\"bibr\\\" rid=\\\"CR12\\\">12</xref>].</p><p id=\\\"Par8\\\">Dupilumab, a fully human monoclonal antibody, targets the IL-4/IL-13 signaling to inhibit a major source of inflammation associated with AD. Since its approval in 2020 by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), dupilumab has been used to treat moderate-to-severe AD in China. 611 is a recombinant humanized immunoglobulin-G4 (IgG4) monoclonal antibody that inhibits IL-4 and IL-13 signaling. Preclinical and phase 1 clinical studies have validated the safety and tolerability of subcutaneous administration of 611 in healthy subjects. This phase 2 study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of 611 in patients with moderate-to-severe AD.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"Sec2\\\"><title>Methods</title><sec id=\\\"Sec3\\\"><title>Study Design, Patients, and Treatment</title><p id=\\\"Par9\\\">This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (ClinicalTrials.gov, <ext-link xmlns:xlink=\\\"http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink\\\" ext-link-type=\\\"pmc:clinical-trial\\\" xlink:href=\\\"NCT05544591\\\">NCT05544591</ext-link>) was conducted across 23 sites in China. This study adhered to the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki for medical research involving human subjects and was conducted in accordance with Good Clinical Practice (GCP) guidelines. Before the study commenced, the clinical trial protocol, case report forms, informed consent forms, and other related documents were approved by the Peking University People’s Hospital Ethics Committee (approval number: 2022PHC022-001). All patients provided written informed consent for participation in the study. The study duration for each participant was 28 weeks, including a screening period of up to 4 weeks, a 16-week treatment period, and an 8-week follow-up period. Patients aged 18–75 years with moderate-to-severe AD were enrolled. Inclusion criteria included a baseline Investigator’s Global Assessment (IGA) score of ≥ 3, Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) score of ≥ 16, ≥ 10% body surface area (BSA) of AD involvement, and a weekly average peak pruritus numerical rating scale (NRS) score of ≥ 4. Detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria are outlined in Supplementary Table S1. After screening, eligible subjects were stratified by IGA scores (3 or 4) and randomly assigned in a 1:1:1 ratio to the following groups: Group A (611 300 mg every 2 weeks with a 600 mg loading dose), Group B (611 300 mg every 4 weeks with a 600 mg loading dose), or placebo. All participants used emollients at least 7 days before randomization and continued this regimen throughout the study.</p></sec><sec id=\\\"Sec4\\\"><title>Endpoints and Assessments</title><sec id=\\\"Sec5\\\"><title>Efficacy Assessments</title><p id=\\\"Par10\\\">The primary efficacy endpoint was the proportion of patients achieving at least a 75% reduction in the Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI-75) score at week 16. Secondary endpoints included the proportion of participants achieving EASI-50, EASI-90, IGA score of 0 or 1 (0/1) with ≥ 2 point reduction, and ≥ 4 points or ≥ 3 points in the weekly average peak pruritus NRS score from baseline to week 16. The Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) and Patient-Oriented Eczema Measure (POEM) were also evaluated. (A list of all efficacy endpoints is provided in Supplementary Table S2).</p></sec><sec id=\\\"Sec6\\\"><title>Safety Assessments</title><p id=\\\"Par11\\\">Safety assessment included treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs), vital signs, physical examinations, electrocardiograms (ECGs), and clinical laboratory test results.</p></sec></sec><sec id=\\\"Sec7\\\"><title>Biological Markers</title><p id=\\\"Par12\\\">Pharmacodynamic markers included TARC, total serum IgE, peripheral blood eosinophil count (EOS), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH).</p></sec><sec id=\\\"Sec8\\\"><title>Statistical Analysis</title><p id=\\\"Par13\\\">The sample size calculation was based on the primary endpoint (the percentage of subjects achieving an EASI-75 response at week 16). Assuming EASI-75 response rates of 49.2% for 611 and 11.5% for the placebo group at week 16, a sample size of 90 subjects with a randomization ratio of 1:1:1 was required to achieve a stated power of 80% to show superiority of 611 over placebo at a significance level of <italic toggle=\\\"yes\\\">α</italic> = 0.05 (two-sided) accounting for a 10% dropout rate. The calculation is based on Fisher’s exact test for the binomial distribution using PASS 2019 software.</p><p id=\\\"Par14\\\">The primary analysis and binary endpoints were conducted in the Intent-to-Treat (ITT) analysis set, which included all randomized subjects, using the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) test adjusted for stratification factors [baseline IGA score (3 or 4)] to compare the proportions of subjects between treatment groups. Intercurrent events, including the use of rescue therapy, administration of prohibited medications affecting the interpretation, or discontinuation of treatment due to lack of efficacy, were classified as non-responders from that time. Missing data were imputed using the non-responder imputation (NRI).</p><p id=\\\"Par15\\\">For continuous efficacy endpoints (e.g., a change from baseline in EASI score), an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model was employed to estimate the least square means (LSM) of changes from baseline to week 16 while controlling for baseline covariates and stratification factors. The intercurrent events, similar to the primary endpoint, were considered missing and imputed using the baseline observation carried forward (BOCF) from that time. Missing data were imputed using multiple imputation (MI), and the statistical inferences obtained from all imputed data were combined using Rubin’s rule. Safety analysis was conducted using descriptive statistics in the safety population, including all randomized subjects who received investigational drugs by treatment group.</p></sec></sec><sec id=\\\"Sec9\\\"><title>Results</title><sec id=\\\"Sec10\\\"><title>Baseline Characteristics</title><p id=\\\"Par16\\\">A total of 120 subjects were screened, and 30, 31, and 32 subjects were assigned to Group A, Group B, and the placebo group, respectively (Fig. <xref rid=\\\"Fig1\\\" ref-type=\\\"fig\\\">1</xref>). Nine patients withdrew from the study predominantly because of lack of efficacy (1 patient each in Groups A and B, and 7 patients in the placebo group).<fig id=\\\"Fig1\\\" position=\\\"float\\\" orientation=\\\"portrait\\\"><label>Fig. 1</label><caption><p>Patient disposition. data-article-body=\\\\\\\"true\\\\\\\" data-track-component=\\\\\\\"article body\\\\\\\" class=\\\\\\\"c-article-body\\\\\\\">\\\\n\\\\n                    \\\\n                    <section aria-labelledby=\\\\\\\"Abs1\\\\\\\" data-title=\\\\\\\"Abstract\\\\\\\" lang=\\\\\\\"en\\\\\\\"><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Abs1-section\\\\\\\"><h2 class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Abs1\\\\\\\">Abstract</h2><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__content\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Abs1-content\\\\\\\"><h3 class=\\\\\\\"c-article__sub-heading\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"abstract-sub-heading\\\\\\\">Background</h3><p>SHR-1819 is a novel monoclonal antibody targeting IL-4Rα, developed for the treatment of type 2 inflammatory diseases such as atopic dermatitis (AD). This phase 2 study aimed to evaluate SHR-1819 for treating moderate-to-severe AD.</p><h3 class=\\\\\\\"c-article__sub-heading\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"abstract-sub-heading\\\\\\\">Methods</h3><p>Patients with an Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) score ≥ 16, an Investigator’s Global Assessment (IGA) score ≥ 3, and ≥ 10% body surface area affected by AD were randomized (1:1:1:1) to receive SHR-1819 at 300 mg every 2 weeks (Q2W), 600 mg Q2W, 600 mg every 4 weeks (Q4W), or placebo for 16 weeks. Patients were required to use topical moisturizer at least 7 days before randomization, twice daily, and continuously throughout the entire study period. Primary endpoint was the proportion of patients achieving a ≥ 75% reduction from baseline in EASI score (EASI-75) at week 16.</p><h3 class=\\\\\\\"c-article__sub-heading\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"abstract-sub-heading\\\\\\\">Results</h3><p>A total of 157 patients received treatment (<i>n</i> = 39, 40, and 41 in the SHR-1819 300 mg Q2W, 600 mg Q2W, and 600 mg Q4W groups; <i>n</i> = 37 in the placebo group). At week 16, the EASI-75 rate was numerically higher in the SHR-1819 groups, compared with the placebo group (69.2% [95% CI: 53.6%-81.4%] at 300 mg Q2W, 75.0% [95% CI: 59.8%-85.8%] at 600 mg Q2W, and 85.4% [95% CI: 71.6%-93.1%] at 600 mg Q4W vs. 37.8% [95% CI: 24.1%-53.9%]; all nominal <i>p</i> &lt; 0.01). Compared with placebo, more patients treated with SHR-1819 achieved IGA score 0–1 and ≥ 2 points reduction, and had ≥ 4 points reduction in weekly average daily Peak Pruritus Numerical Rating Scale score. Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were comparable between the SHR-1819 and placebo groups (45.8% vs. 40.5%). The most common TRAE with SHR-1819 was injection site reaction (10.8%), increased blood bilirubin (5.8%), and conjunctivitis (5.0%). Dose-proportional increases in SHR-1819 concentrations were observed within the studied range. SHR-1819 revealed notable reductions in thymus and activation-regulated chemokine, immunoglobulin E, and eotaxin-3 levels across all doses.</p><h3 class=\\\\\\\"c-article__sub-heading\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"abstract-sub-heading\\\\\\\">Conclusions</h3><p>SHR-1819 demonstrated promising efficacy in improving the signs and symptoms of AD, with a well-tolerated safety profile and favorable pharmacokinetic, and pharmacodynamic characteristics.</p><h3 class=\\\\\\\"c-article__sub-heading\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"abstract-sub-heading\\\\\\\">Trial Registration</h3><p>ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05549947; registered on September 22, 2022.</p></div></div></section>\\\\n\\\\n                    \\\\n                        \\\\n    \\\\n    <div class=\\\\\\\"app-nls-widget <section data-title=\\\\\\\"Background\\\\\\\"><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec1-section\\\\\\\"><h2 class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec1\\\\\\\">Background</h2><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__content\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec1-content\\\\\\\"><p>Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by pruritic and eczematous lesions [<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" aria-label=\\\\\\\"Reference 1\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Langan SM, Irvine AD, Weidinger S. Atopic dermatitis. Lancet. 2020;396:345–60.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR1\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e1171\\\\\\\">1</a>, <a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" aria-label=\\\\\\\"Reference 2\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Weidinger S, Novak N. Atopic dermatitis. Lancet. 2016;387:1109–22.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR2\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e1174\\\\\\\">2</a>]. The burden of AD extends beyond physical symptoms, as patients living with this condition often experience a profound impact on their mental health due to the psychological and social challenges it presents [<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Drucker AM, Wang AR, Li WQ, Sevetson E, Block JK, Qureshi AA. The Burden of Atopic Dermatitis: Summary of a Report for the National Eczema Association. J Invest Dermatol. 2017;137:26–30.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"#ref-CR3\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e1177\\\\\\\">3</a>,<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Carroll CL, Balkrishnan R, Feldman SR, Fleischer AB Jr., Manuel JC. The burden of atopic dermatitis: impact on the patient, family, and society. Pediatr Dermatol. 2005;22:192–9.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"#ref-CR4\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e1177_1\\\\\\\">4</a>,<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Drucker AM. Atopic dermatitis: Burden of illness, quality of life, and associated complications. Allergy Asthma Proc. 2017; 38:3–8.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"#ref-CR5\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e1177_2\\\\\\\">5</a>,<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" aria-label=\\\\\\\"Reference 6\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Ali F, Vyas J, Finlay AY. Counting the Burden: Atopic Dermatitis and Health-related Quality of Life. Acta Derm Venereol. 2020;100:adv00161.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR6\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e1180\\\\\\\">6</a>].</p><p>Traditional treatments for AD, such as topical corticosteroids and systemic immunosuppressants, have been the cornerstone of therapy for many years [<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Ring J, Alomar A, Bieber T, Deleuran M, Fink-Wagner A, Gelmetti C, et al. Guidelines for treatment of atopic eczema (atopic dermatitis) Part II. J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol. 2012;26:1176–93.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"#ref-CR9\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e1186_2\\\\\\\">9</a>,<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Sidbury R, Davis DM, Cohen DE, Cordoro KM, Berger TG, Bergman JN, et al. The IL-4, IL-13 and IL-31 pathways in atopic dermatitis. Expert Rev Clin Immunol. 2021;17:835–52.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR14\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e1198\\\\\\\">14</a>]. IL-4 inhibition via blockade of IL-4 receptor alpha (IL-4Rα), a receptor shared by IL-4 and IL-13, represents a well-established target for AD. Monoclonal antibodies that target IL-4Rα have the potential to block the biological effects of both IL-4 and IL-13 simultaneously, providing a more comprehensive and effective treatment approach compared with agents that selectively target either cytokine pathway [<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" aria-label=\\\\\\\"Reference 15\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"May RD, Fung M. Strategies targeting the IL-4/IL-13 axes in disease. Cytokine. 2015;75:89–116.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR15\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e1201\\\\\\\">15</a>, <a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" aria-label=\\\\\\\"Reference 16\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Gandhi NA, Pirozzi G, Graham NMH. Expert Rev Clin Immunol. 2017;13:425–37.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR16\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e1204\\\\\\\">16</a>]. Dupilumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting IL-4Rα, has emerged as a frontrunner and has received approval from the U.S. FDA for the treatment of AD [<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Paller AS, Siegfried EC, Thaci D, Wollenberg A, Cork MJ, Arkwright PD, et al. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2020;83:1282–93.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"#ref-CR17\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e1207\\\\\\\">17</a>,<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Simpson EL, Paller AS, Siegfried EC, Boguniewicz M, Sher L, Gooderham MJ, et al. JAMA Dermatol. 2020;156:44–56.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"#ref-CR18\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e1207_1\\\\\\\">18</a>,<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Simpson EL, Bieber T, Guttman-Yassky E, Beck LA, Blauvelt A, Cork MJ, et al. Dupilumab in patients with prurigo nodularis: two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that SHR-1819 exhibits high affinity for human and marmoset IL-4Rα and shows promising biological activity in relevant animal models of AD, rhinitis, and asthma (Data on file, Hengrui). Moreover, SHR-1819 has demonstrated similar inhibitory activity and receptor occupancy profiles to dupilumab against hIL-4/hIL-4Rα in vivo (Data on file, Hengrui). In a first-in-human phase 1 trial involving healthy participants, SHR-1819 was well-tolerated, displayed exposure increasing in a dose-proportional manner, and led to modest reductions in inflammatory biomarkers such as thymus and activation-regulated chemokine/CC chemokine ligand 17 (TARC/CCL17) and immunoglobulin E (IgE) [<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" aria-label=\\\\\\\"Reference 28\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Li N, Shakib S, Qian W, Yao X, Li P, Nip TK, et al. Safety, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of anti-IL-4Ralpha antibody SHR-1819 in healthy subjects: A randomized, controlled phase I study. Clin Transl Sci. 2024;17:e13763.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR28\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e1223\\\\\\\">28</a>]. In this context, we conducted this phase 2 study to investigate the efficacy, safety, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of SHR-1819 in patients with moderate-to-severe AD.</p></div></div></section><section data-title=\\\\\\\"Methods\\\\\\\"><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec2-section\\\\\\\"><h2 class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec2\\\\\\\">Methods</h2><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__content\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec2-content\\\\\\\"><h3 class=\\\\\\\"c-article__sub-heading\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec3\\\\\\\">Study design and patients</h3><p>This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial was conducted in 22 centers in China (ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05549947).</p><p>Patients aged 18–75 years and had been diagnosed with AD in accordance with the 2014 American Academy of Dermatology guidelines for a minimum of one year prior to screening were enrolled [<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" aria-label=\\\\\\\"Reference 29\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Eichenfield LF, Tom WL, Chamlin SL, Feldman SR, Hanifin JM, Simpson EL, et al. Guidelines of care for the management of atopic dermatitis: Sect.  1. Diagnosis and assessment of atopic dermatitis. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2014;70:338–51.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR29\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e1241\\\\\\\">29</a>]. Eligible patients were required to have moderate-to-severe AD, as indicated by an Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) score of ≥ 16, an Investigator’s Global Assessment (IGA) score of ≥ 3, and a Body Surface Area (BSA) involvement of ≥ 10%. Moreover, patients should have an average of the daily Peak Pruritus Numerical Rating Scale (PP-NRS) score of ≥ 4 over the 7 days preceding randomization and meet at least one of following criteria: suboptimal response to moderate or higher potency topical corticosteroids, prior use of systemic therapy (such as systemic corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, or Janus kinase inhibitors) regardless of treatment response, or ineligibility for topical therapy. Key exclusion criteria are provided in the supplementary methods.</p><p>The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the Good Clinical Practice Guideline. Protocol received approval from the institutional review board or independent ethics committee of each study center. All participants provided written informed consent before enrollment.</p><h3 class=\\\\\\\"c-article__sub-heading\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec4\\\\\\\">Procedures</h3><p>Patients were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) to receive SHR-1819 at 300 mg every 2 weeks (Q2W), 600 mg Q2W, 600 mg every 4 weeks (Q4W), or placebo for 16 weeks. A 600 mg initial loading dose was used in the 300 mg Q2W group to expedite the attainment of target concentration levels and accelerate the onset of drug efficacy. This study employed a stratified block randomization method with a block size of 8, stratified by disease severity (moderate [IGA = 3] vs. severe [IGA = 4]). Randomization was performed via a centralized randomization system, under which participating sites competitively enrolled subjects. A dedicated randomization specialist generated the random allocation sequence and drug numbering table using SAS software. The centralized randomization system assigned eligible participants to treatment groups, and corresponding investigational products were dispensed according to the randomization results. All study treatments were prepared as visually identical injectable formulations to maintain blinding, thereby ensuring that patients, investigators, and the sponsor were all kept unaware of the treatment assignment. Requirements for concomitant medications and rescue treatments are provided in the supplementary methods.</p><h3 class=\\\\\\\"c-article__sub-heading\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec5\\\\\\\">Outcomes and assessments</h3><p>The primary endpoint was the proportion of patients achieving ≥ 75% reduction from baseline in EASI score (EASI-75) at week 16. Secondary efficacy endpoints, also assessed at week 16, included the proportion of patients with an IGA score of 0 or 1 (on a 0–4 scale) and a reduction of ≥ 2 points from baseline; the proportion of patients with a reduction of ≥ 2 points in IGA score from baseline; the proportion of patients achieving EASI-90 (EASI score reduction of ≥ 90% from baseline); the proportion of patients achieving EASI-50 (EASI score reduction of ≥ 50% from baseline); the proportion of patients with a reduction of ≥ 4 points from baseline in weekly average of the daily PP-NRS score; as well as the absolute and percentage changes from baseline in EASI score, Scoring Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD) score, BSA affected by AD, and Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) score. Other secondary endpoints were safety; pharmacokinetics (PK); pharmacodynamics (PD; including TARC/CCL17, IgE, and eotaxin-3 levels and their percentage change from baseline); and immunogenicity.</p><p>Adverse events (AEs) were classified according to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities, version 26.0.</p><p>The serum concentration of SHR-1819, TARC/CCL17, and eotaxin-3 levels were quantified using an established enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay method at Shanghai TriApex Biotechnology Co., Ltd. IgE concentrations were measured using the Atellica IM Total IgE assay at the ACL laboratory in the CMAX clinical facility. Anti-drug antibodies (ADAs) were analyzed using electrochemiluminescence at Shanghai TriApex Biotechnology Co., Ltd.</p><h3 class=\\\\\\\"c-article__sub-heading\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec6\\\\\\\">Statistical analysis</h3><p>Assuming an EASI-75 rate at week 16 of 15% in the placebo group and maximum 50% among the three SHR-1819 groups, 37 participants per group (148 in total) could provide the study with 85% power to detect the difference between SHR-1819 and placebo, with a two-sided significance level of 0.05 and an anticipated dropout rate of 15% per group.</p><p>For the primary endpoint, the proportions of patients achieving EASI-75 at week 16 were calculated, with 95% confidence intervals (CI) estimated using the Wilson method. Between-group differences in the proportions and their 95% CIs were estimated using the stratified Mantel-Haenszel method. The stratified Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel method was utilized to compare each dose of SHR-1819 with placebo in the proportion of patients achieving EASI-75 at week 16, and to report the two-sided p-value. When participants discontinued the study treatment, a treatment strategy was adopted (i.e. the data collected in subsequent follow-up visits were included in analysis). When participants received rescue medication, a composite strategy was employed (i.e. the participant was considered as not achieving EASI-75 at week 16). The missing data were imputed using the non-responder imputation (NRI) method (i.e. the participant was considered as not achieving EASI-75 at week 16).</p><p>The same methods as those for the primary endpoint were applied to analyze dichotomous secondary endpoints at week 16. For continuous endpoints at week 16, a mixed-effects model repeated measures (MMRM) analysis was conducted using the restricted estimation maximum likelihood approach. In the MMRM model, baseline scores were used as covariates, with random stratification factors, treatment group, visit, and the interaction between treatment group and visit as fixed effects. The covariance matrix could be either unstructured or compound symmetry as alternative. Intercurrent events were not considered for all secondary endpoints. The missing data for dichotomous secondary endpoints were imputed using the NRI method, while continuous endpoints were handled by the MMRM model.</p><p>All p values are nominal, presented for descriptive and exploratory purposes, and were not adjusted for multiple comparisons. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize baseline characteristics, safety data, PK, PD, and ADA results. Statistical analyses were primarily conducted using SAS version 9.4 or above. See Additional file <a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"supplementary material anchor\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#MOESM1\\\\\\\">1</a> for statistical analysis plan.</p></div></div></section><section data-title=\\\\\\\"Results\\\\\\\"><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec7-section\\\\\\\"><h2 class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec7\\\\\\\">Results</h2><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__content\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec7-content\\\\\\\"><h3 class=\\\\\\\"c-article__sub-heading\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec8\\\\\\\">Patients</h3><p>From October 26, 2022, to May 26, 2023, 192 patients were screened and 158 eligible patients were randomly assigned. A total of 157 patients received the assigned treatment, with 39, 40, 41, and 37 patients in the SHR-1819 300 mg Q2W, 600 mg Q2W, 600 mg Q4W, and placebo groups, respectively (Fig. <a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"figure anchor\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Fig1\\\\\\\">1</a>). As of database lock (November 23, 2023), 145 patients completed their assigned treatment.</p><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"figure\\\\\\\" data-container-section=\\\\\\\"figure\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"figure-1\\\\\\\" data-title=\\\\\\\"Fig. 1\\\\\\\"><figure><figcaption><b id=\\\\\\\"Fig1\\\\\\\" class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__figure-caption\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"figure-caption-text\\\\\\\">Fig. 1</b></figcaption><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__figure-content\\\\\\\"><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__figure-item\\\\\\\"><picture class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__figure-picture\\\\\\\"><img aria-describedby=\\\\\\\"figure-1-desc\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1186%2Fs12916-026-04952-3/MediaObjects/12916_2026_4952_Fig1_HTML.png\\\\\\\" alt=\\\\\\\"Fig. 1\\\\\\\" loading=\\\\\\\"lazy\\\\\\\" width=\\\\\\\"685\\\\\\\" height=\\\\\\\"304\\\\\\\"></picture><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__figure-link\\\\\\\"><a class=\\\\\\\"c-article__pill-button\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"article-link\\\\\\\" data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"button\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"view figure\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3/figures/1\\\\\\\" data-track-dest=\\\\\\\"link:Figure1 Full size image\\\\\\\" aria-label=\\\\\\\"Full size image figure 1\\\\\\\" rel=\\\\\\\"nofollow\\\\\\\"><span>Full size image</span><svg width=\\\\\\\"16\\\\\\\" height=\\\\\\\"16\\\\\\\" focusable=\\\\\\\"false\\\\\\\" role=\\\\\\\"img\\\\\\\" aria-hidden=\\\\\\\"true\\\\\\\" class=\\\\\\\"u-icon\\\\\\\"><use xmlns:xlink=\\\\\\\"http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink\\\\\\\" xlink:href=\\\\\\\"#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small\\\\\\\"></use></svg></a></div></div><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__figure-description\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"bottom-caption\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"figure-1-desc\\\\\\\"><p>Patient disposition. Q2W, every 2 weeks; Q4W, every 4 weeks</p></div></div></figure></div><p>The demographics and clinical characterization at baseline were well-balanced across groups (Table <a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"table anchor\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Tab1\\\\\\\">1</a>). In the SHR-1819 and placebo groups, 60.0% (72/120) and 62.2% (23/37) of patients had AD lasting ≥ 5 years, respectively.</p><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-table\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"inline-table\\\\\\\" data-container-section=\\\\\\\"table\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"table-1\\\\\\\"><figure><figcaption class=\\\\\\\"c-article-table__figcaption\\\\\\\"><b id=\\\\\\\"Tab1\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"table-caption\\\\\\\">Table 1 Demographics and baseline characteristics</b></figcaption><div class=\\\\\\\"u-text-right u-hide-print\\\\\\\"><a class=\\\\\\\"c-article__pill-button\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"table-link\\\\\\\" data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"view table\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"button\\\\\\\" rel=\\\\\\\"nofollow\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3/tables/1\\\\\\\" aria-label=\\\\\\\"Full size table 1\\\\\\\"><span>Full size table</span><svg width=\\\\\\\"16\\\\\\\" height=\\\\\\\"16\\\\\\\" focusable=\\\\\\\"false\\\\\\\" role=\\\\\\\"img\\\\\\\" aria-hidden=\\\\\\\"true\\\\\\\" class=\\\\\\\"u-icon\\\\\\\"><use xmlns:xlink=\\\\\\\"http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink\\\\\\\" xlink:href=\\\\\\\"#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small\\\\\\\"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div><p>A total of 17 patients received rescue treatment in this study: 12 during the treatment period and 5 during the safety follow‑up period. Rescue treatment was administered to 4 (10.3%), 1 (2.5%), and 12 (32.4%) patients in the SHR‑1819 300 mg Q2W, 600 mg Q2W, and placebo groups, respectively; no patients in the 600 mg Q4W group received rescue treatment. Among those who received rescue treatment, the majority received topical agents, with only 1 (5.9%) patient in the placebo group requiring systemic therapy.</p><h3 class=\\\\\\\"c-article__sub-heading\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec10\\\\\\\">Efficacy</h3><p>The proportion of patients achieving EASI-75 at week 16 in all three SHR-1819 groups (300 mg Q2W: 69.2% [95% CI: 53.6–81.4]; 600 mg Q2W: 75.0% [95% CI: 59.8–85.8]; 600 mg Q4W: 85.4% [95% CI: 71.6–93.1]) was numerically higher than that in the placebo group (37.8% [95% CI: 24.1–53.9]), with differences of 31.6% (95% CI: 10.3–53.0; nominal <i>p</i> = 0.006), 37.0% (95% CI: 16.3–57.6; nominal <i>p</i> = 0.001), and 47.4% (95% CI: 28.3–66.4; nominal <i>p</i> &lt; 0.001), respectively (Fig. <a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"figure anchor\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Fig2\\\\\\\">2</a>A). The 600 mg Q4W group exhibited the highest EASI-75 response rate among the three SHR-1819 groups at week 16 (Fig. <a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"figure anchor\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Fig2\\\\\\\">2</a>B). Subgroup analysis demonstrated that a trend favoring SHR-1819 over placebo in EASI‑75 response rate was observed across most prespecified subgroups, with nominal <i>p</i> &lt; 0.05 in multiple subgroups for each dose regimen (Additional file 2: Figure S<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"supplementary material anchor\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#MOESM2\\\\\\\">1</a>). </p><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__figure js-c-reading-companion-figures-item\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"figure\\\\\\\" nominal <i>p</i> = 0.010, = 0.031, and &lt; 0.001; Fig. <a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"figure anchor\\\\\\\" Additionally, a greater proportion of patients in the SHR-1819 groups achieved an EASI-50 response compared with the placebo group (86.4%, 92.5%, 97.6% vs. 54.1%; nominal <i>p</i> = 0.004, &lt; 0.001, and &lt; 0.001; Fig. <a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"figure anchor\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Fig2\\\\\\\">2</a>A).</p><p>Treatment with SHR-1819 also led to a higher percentage of patients achieving a reduction of ≥ 4 points in weekly average of the daily PP-NRS score from baseline at week 16 compared with placebo (41.0%, 47.5%, and 43.9% vs. 16.2%; nominal <i>p</i> = 0.017, 0.004, and 0.007; Fig. <a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"figure anchor\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Fig3\\\\\\\">3</a>A and C).</p><p>Furthermore, all three doses of SHR-1819 resulted in a reduction at week 16 from baseline in the SCORAD index, BSA affected by AD, and DLQI score compared with placebo (Additional file 2: Table S<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"supplementary material anchor\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#MOESM2\\\\\\\">1</a>).</p><h3 class=\\\\\\\"c-article__sub-heading\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec12\\\\\\\">Safety</h3><p>AEs were reported in 105 (87.5%) of 120 patients treated with SHR-1819 and 30 (81.1%) of 37 patients with placebo (Table <a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"table anchor\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Tab2\\\\\\\">2</a>). The majority were mild or moderate in severity (83.3% with SHR-1819 and 73.0% with placebo), while severe AEs were reported in 4.2% and 8.1% of the patients with SHR-1819 and placebo, respectively. Commonly reported AEs in patients receiving SHR-1819 included upper respiratory tract infection (22.5%), injection site reaction (10.8%), COVID-19 (9.2%), hyperlipidemia (9.2%), increased alanine aminotransferase (8.3%), and hyperuricemia (8.3%). Notably, the incidence and severity of AEs did not show an association with higher doses of SHR-1819.</p><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-table\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"inline-table\\\\\\\" data-container-section=\\\\\\\"table\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"table-2\\\\\\\"><figure><figcaption class=\\\\\\\"c-article-table__figcaption\\\\\\\"><b id=\\\\\\\"Tab2\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"table-caption\\\\\\\">Table 2 Safety results</b></figcaption><div class=\\\\\\\"u-text-right u-hide-print\\\\\\\"><a class=\\\\\\\"c-article__pill-button\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"table-link\\\\\\\" data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"view table\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"button\\\\\\\" rel=\\\\\\\"nofollow\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3/tables/2\\\\\\\" aria-label=\\\\\\\"Full size table 2\\\\\\\"><span>Full size table</span><svg width=\\\\\\\"16\\\\\\\" height=\\\\\\\"16\\\\\\\" focusable=\\\\\\\"false\\\\\\\" role=\\\\\\\"img\\\\\\\" aria-hidden=\\\\\\\"true\\\\\\\" class=\\\\\\\"u-icon\\\\\\\"><use xmlns:xlink=\\\\\\\"http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink\\\\\\\" xlink:href=\\\\\\\"#icon-eds-i-chevron-right-small\\\\\\\"></use></svg></a></div></figure></div><p>Treatment-related AEs (TRAEs) occurred in 55 (45.8%) patients in the SHR-1819 groups and 15 (40.5%) patients in the placebo group (Table <a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"table anchor\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#Tab2\\\\\\\">2</a>). Injection site reaction (10.8%), increased blood bilirubin (5.8%), conjunctivitis (5.0%), increased blood uric acid (4.2%), and increased alanine aminotransferase (4.2%) were among the most commonly reported TRAEs in the SHR-1819 group. The majority of TRAEs with SHR-1819 treatment were mild in 40 (33.3%) patients and moderate in 14 (11.7%) patients, with only 1 (0.8%) patient experiencing severe TRAE. The incidence and severity of TRAEs were not correlated with the dosage of SHR-1819.</p><p>Treatment interruptions due to AEs were reported in 8 (6.7%) patients in the SHR-1819 group and 2 (5.4%) in the placebo group. Treatment discontinuations resulting from AEs were reported in 1 (0.8%) patient from the SHR-1819 group and 1 (2.7%) from the placebo group. Serious AEs were noted in 7 (5.8%) patients in the SHR-1819 group and 3 (8.1%) in the placebo group (Additional file 2: Table S<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"supplementary material anchor\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#MOESM2\\\\\\\">2</a>). Among these serious AEs, 2 (1.3%, dermatitis atopic) were considered treatment-related, with 1 (0.8%) in the SHR-1819 group and 1 (2.7%) in the placebo group. One patient from the SHR-1819 Q4W group died due to AE (brain herniation), and this event was not deemed treatment-related.</p><p>Conjunctivitis occurred in 7 patients (5.8%; all in the SHR-1819 group), including 6 treatment-related events (5.0%). Severity distribution comprised 4 mild and 3 moderate events. Complete resolution was observed in 6 patients (85.7%), and no treatment discontinuations were attributed to conjunctivitis. The majority of laboratory abnormalities were mild, with 7 patients of moderate abnormalities; no severe laboratory abnormalities were observed. All were managed without intervention and resolved or recovered completely.</p><h3 class=\\\\\\\"c-article__sub-heading\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec13\\\\\\\">PK</h3><p>A total of 120 patients were included in the PK analysis. The serum concentration of SHR-1819 gradually increased over the treatment period. The serum drug concentration in the 600 mg Q2W group was higher than those in both the 300 mg Q2W and 600 mg Q4W groups (Additional file 2: Figure S<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"supplementary material anchor\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#MOESM2\\\\\\\">2</a>).</p><h3 class=\\\\\\\"c-article__sub-heading\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec14\\\\\\\">PD</h3><p>PD analysis was conducted on all 157 patients. SHR-1819 produced a notable decrease in IgE levels across all doses. With multiple administration of SHR-1819, the median percentage decrease in IgE concentration from baseline increased steadily, and maintained until the end of the follow-up period (Additional file 2: Figure S<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"supplementary material anchor\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#MOESM2\\\\\\\">3</a>A). Similarly, the median percentage reduction from baseline in TARC/CCL17 reached a plateau in 2 weeks after SHR-1819 administration and was sustained until approximately 8 weeks after the last dose (Additional file 2: Figure S<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"supplementary material anchor\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#MOESM2\\\\\\\">3</a>B). The reduction from baseline in serum eotaxin-3 levels was evident in all SHR-1819 groups starting from week 2 of the treatment period, and this reduction was maintained during the first 4 weeks following the last dose (Additional file 2: Figure S<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"supplementary material anchor\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#MOESM2\\\\\\\">3</a>C). There was no clear indication of a dose-dependent reduction in IgE and eotaxin-3 levels across different doses, whereas 600 mg Q2W SHR-1819 demonstrated a slightly lower reduction in TARC/CCL17. Exposure-response modeling indicated no obvious correlation between baseline PD biomarkers and clinical endpoints.</p><h3 class=\\\\\\\"c-article__sub-heading\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec15\\\\\\\">Immunogenicity</h3><p>ADA positivity was detected in 3 (7.7%), 2 (5.0%), and 4 (9.8%) patients following SHR-1819 at 300 mg Q2W, 600 mg Q2W, and 600 mg Q4W. There was no discernible relationship between the occurrence of ADA positivity and the SHR-1819 dose.</p></div></div></section><section data-title=\\\\\\\"Discussion\\\\\\\"><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec16-section\\\\\\\"><h2 class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec16\\\\\\\">Discussion</h2><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__content\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec16-content\\\\\\\"><p>This phase 2 study demonstrated that SHR-1819 is an effective treatment for moderate-to-severe AD. SHR-1819 produced promising improvements in EASI, IGA, PP-NRS, SCORAD index, BSA affected by AD, and DLQI compared with placebo, indicating efficacy in ameliorating disease severity and alleviating symptoms of AD. SHR-1819 was well-tolerated, and the PK and PD profiles were favorable.</p><p>Dupilumab, an anti-IL-4Rα monoclonal antibody, demonstrated promising improvements in EASI response in the SOLO 1 and SOLO 2 trials (EASI-75 rate: 51% and 44%; EASI-90 rate: 36% and 30%; and EASI-50 rate: 69% and 65%, at week 16) [<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" aria-label=\\\\\\\"Reference 19\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Simpson EL, Bieber T, Guttman-Yassky E, Beck LA, Blauvelt A, Cork MJ, et al. Two Phase 3 Trials of Dupilumab versus Placebo in Atopic Dermatitis. N Engl J Med. 2016;375:2335–48.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR19\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e3191\\\\\\\">19</a>]. In our study, the proportion of patients achieving EASI-75 (69.2%-85.4%), EASI-90 (53.8%-63.4%), and EASI-50 (84.6%-97.6%) responses at week 16 was numerically higher in the SHR-1819 groups compared with placebo, with the 600 mg Q4W group showing the most substantial improvements. Despite cross-trial comparison should be interpreted with caution due to differences in study design and patient populations, our results preliminarily indicated that SHR-1819 could be a promising treatment choice for moderate-to-severe AD.</p><p>The substantial reduction observed in the PP-NRS score further highlights the beneficial effects of SHR-1819 on pruritus, a hallmark symptom of AD that markedly impacts the quality of life of patients. Moreover, reductions in other efficacy endpoints including IGA scores, SCORAD index, BSA affected by AD, and DLQI score underscore the comprehensive efficacy of SHR-1819 in improving multiple aspects of the disease burden.</p><p>The efficacy of SHR-1819 provides a promising new treatment option for patients with moderate-to-severe AD and offers flexibility in choosing either Q2W or Q4W dosing regimens. The ability to achieve substantial clinical improvement with a once-monthly dosing regimen may offer convenience for patients.</p><p>The safety profile of SHR-1819 was generally favorable and aligned with the biologic therapies targeting IL-4Rα [<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" aria-label=\\\\\\\"Reference 19\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Simpson EL, Bieber T, Guttman-Yassky E, Beck LA, Blauvelt A, Cork MJ, et al. Two Phase 3 Trials of Dupilumab versus Placebo in Atopic Dermatitis. N Engl J Med. 2016;375:2335–48.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR19\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e3204\\\\\\\">19</a>, <a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Thaci D, Simpson EL, Beck LA, Bieber T, Blauvelt A, Papp K, et al. Efficacy and safety of dupilumab in adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis inadequately controlled by topical treatments: a randomised, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging phase 2b trial. Lancet. 2016;387:40–52.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"#ref-CR30\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e3207\\\\\\\">30</a>,<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Zhao Y, Wu L, Lu Q, Gao X, Zhu X, Yao X, et al. The efficacy and safety of dupilumab in Chinese patients with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Br J Dermatol. 2022;186:633–41.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"#ref-CR31\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e3207_1\\\\\\\">31</a>,<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Paller AS, Silverberg JI, Cork MJ, Guttman-Yassky E, Lockshin B, Irvine AD, et al. Efficacy and Safety of Dupilumab in Patients With Erythrodermic Atopic Dermatitis: A Post Hoc Analysis of 6 Randomized Clinical Trials. JAMA Dermatol. 2023;159:255–66.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"#ref-CR32\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e3207_2\\\\\\\">32</a>,<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Gooderham MJ, Hong HC, Eshtiaghi P, Papp KA, Dupilumab. A review of its use in the treatment of atopic dermatitis. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2018;78:S28–36.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"#ref-CR33\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e3207_3\\\\\\\">33</a>,<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" aria-label=\\\\\\\"Reference 34\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Beck LA, Thaci D, Hamilton JD, Graham NM, Bieber T, Rocklin R, et al. Dupilumab treatment in adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. N Engl J Med. 2014;371:130–9.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR34\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e3210\\\\\\\">34</a>], with no new signals identified. The majority of AEs were mild to moderate in severity. Most serious AEs were unrelated to SHR-1819. The single case of death resulted from a car accident-induced brain herniation, ruling out death caused by central nervous system diseases or drug allergies.</p><p>Infection- and infestation-related AEs were all mild to moderate, resolving or improving with symptomatic treatment or without intervention. The most commonly reported AE was upper respiratory tract infection (22.5% with SHR-1819 and 10.8% with placebo), but only 1.7% in the SHR-1819 group and 5.4% in the placebo group were treatment-related. Conjunctivitis occurred only in the SHR-1819 group, affecting all dose groups without a clear dose-response pattern, consistent with the incidence of conjunctivitis reported with dupilumab targeting the same pathway [<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" aria-label=\\\\\\\"Reference 19\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Simpson EL, Bieber T, Guttman-Yassky E, Beck LA, Blauvelt A, Cork MJ, et al. Two Phase 3 Trials of Dupilumab versus Placebo in Atopic Dermatitis. N Engl J Med. 2016;375:2335–48.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR19\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e3216\\\\\\\">19</a>]. The incidence of injection site reaction was higher in the SHR-1819 group (10.8%) compared with the placebo group (5.4%), consistent with that with dupilumab [<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" aria-label=\\\\\\\"Reference 34\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Beck LA, Thaci D, Hamilton JD, Graham NM, Bieber T, Rocklin R, et al. Dupilumab treatment in adults with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. N Engl J Med. 2014;371:130–9.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR34\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e3219\\\\\\\">34</a>].</p><p>The drug exposure and PD profiles of SHR-1819 observed in our study align with the known mechanisms of action of IL-4Rα inhibitors [<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" aria-label=\\\\\\\"Reference 35\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Clot PF, Kamal M, Sun J, Xu C, Kong F, Gu Y, et al. Dupilumab pharmacokinetics in Chinese healthy subjects and patients with atopic dermatitis: Results of two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies. Int Immunopharmacol. 2021;99:107985.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR35\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e3225\\\\\\\">35</a>], providing insights into its potential therapeutic effects. The serum concentration of SHR-1819 increased with dose escalation and remained stable with both Q2W and Q4W administration, supporting the potential for sustained therapeutic effects with both dosing regimens. The PD data showed reductions in IgE, TARC/CCL17, and eotaxin-3 levels, which are known to play key roles in the pathophysiology of AD [<a data-track=\\\\\\\"click\\\\\\\" data-track-action=\\\\\\\"reference anchor\\\\\\\" data-track-label=\\\\\\\"link\\\\\\\" data-test=\\\\\\\"citation-ref\\\\\\\" aria-label=\\\\\\\"Reference 36\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Renert-Yuval Y, Thyssen JP, Bissonnette R, Bieber T, Kabashima K, Hijnen D, et al. Biomarkers in atopic dermatitis-a review on behalf of the International Eczema Council. J Allergy Clin Immunol. 2021;147:1174–e11901171.\\\\\\\" href=\\\\\\\"/article/10.1186/s12916-026-04952-3#ref-CR36\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"ref-link-section-d302106207e3228\\\\\\\">36</a>], and their reduction potentially correlates with clinical improvement. Notably, the magnitude of these PD marker reductions was comparable between the 600 mg Q4W and 600 mg Q2W groups, which demonstrated a plateau in PD effect with the 600 mg Q4W regimen. The numerically higher EASI-75 rates observed in the 600 mg Q4W group compared with the 600 mg Q2W group likely reflect random variability related to the limited sample size of this phase 2 study rather than a meaningful difference in therapeutic effect. Additionally, the incidence of ADA positivity was low.</p><p>Despite the promising results, this study has several limitations. First, the duration of the trial (16 weeks) was relatively short, and longer-term studies are needed to confirm the sustained efficacy and safety profile of SHR-1819. Second, the study did not include direct comparisons with other biologics such as dupilumab, and head-to-head comparative studies with dupilumab would provide valuable insights into the relative benefits and risks of these two monoclonal antibodies. Future research should also focus on investigating the potential of SHR-1819 in combination with other therapies, such as topical treatments or other systemic agents, which could provide insights into optimizing treatment regimens for AD. Last, this study was conducted only in China; therefore, the generalizability of the findings to other ethnic and geographic populations requires confirmation in future global studies.</p></div></div></section><section data-title=\\\\\\\"Conclusions\\\\\\\"><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec17-section\\\\\\\"><h2 class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec17\\\\\\\">Conclusions</h2><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__content\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"Sec17-content\\\\\\\"><p>This phase 2 study demonstrates that SHR-1819 is an effective and well-tolerated treatment in Chinese patients with moderate-to-severe AD. The promising improvements in clinical outcomes, combined with favorable safety, PK, and PD profiles, position SHR-1819 as a promising new therapeutic option. Based on our findings, the 300 mg Q2W and 600 mg Q4W dosing regimens were recommended in subsequent phase 3 trials of SHR-1819. Further research is warranted to establish the role of this novel anti-IL-4Rα antibody in the management of AD.</p></div></div></section>\\\\n                                </div>\\\\n                        \\\\n                    \\\\n\\\\n                        \\\\n\\\\n                    \\\\n                        \\\\n                    \\\\n\\\\n                    \\\\n\\\\n                    <section data-title=\\\\\\\"Data availability\\\\\\\"><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"data-availability-section\\\\\\\"><h2 class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__title js-section-title js-c-reading-companion-sections-item\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"data-availability\\\\\\\">Data availability</h2><div class=\\\\\\\"c-article-section__content\\\\\\\" id=\\\\\\\"data-availability-content\\\\\\\">\\\\n              \\\\n              <p>The individual patient data generated during this study will be considered for sharing after the product and indication have been approved by major health authorities. Data may be requested 24 months after study completion. Qualified researchers should submit a proposal to the corresponding authors outlining the reasons for requiring the data. The sponsor will provide the data if the proposal is approved, provided that the requestor signs a data-access agreement. Use of data must comply with the requirements of Human Genetics Resources Administration of China and other country or region–specific regulations.</p>\\\\n            </div></div></section><section
